newsitem.title: PERU: Peru tightens screws on Marxist MRTA rebels.
newsitem.headline: Peru tightens screws on Marxist MRTA rebels.

text.p: Peru's government tightened the screws on Thursday on Marxist rebels who vowed defiance as they held 73 VIP hostages for the 37th day at the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima.

Shortly before dawn, four carpenters arrived to board up one of the diplomatic compound's two entrances and a small hole in the wall used by service staff. Watched by a group of policemen, the carpenters spent about an hour nailing wooden planks across the two access points.

Their action, which followed several days of heightened police activity and a general tightening of security at the site, left only one entrance open. That gate has been used by Red Cross workers, mediators and freed captives.
A police helicopter also flew over the mined and booby- trapped residence several times during the morning.

Hours before, President Alberto Fujimori publicly reiterated the government's refusal to consider the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement's (MRTA) principal demand for the release of about 400 jailed comrades.

"We are not going to allow (government negotiator Domingo) Palermo to go to the negotiating table unless they accept that there will be no release of prisoners," Fujimori said at a meeting with Japanese reporters.

The government's firm line on the MRTA prisoners has become the sticking point in moves to negotiate a solution to the crisis. Both sides say they are willing in principle to talk but the rebels insist they will not sit down until their main demand is included on the agenda.
The MRTA responded to the government's latest moves via the communication methods that have served it best throughout the crisis.
On the internet, the rebels slammed Fujimori as a "dictator" and called on international opinion to help prevent a "massacre" by the government at the residence.
"We have to stop the dictator now. We do not have to suffer five years more," said a new MRTA communique.

A second communique on the internet added that the police activities were "provocations that seek a pretext to justify military intervention ... We ask for the families, the press, human rights organisations and national and international solidarity to help prevent this massacre we warn of."
Continuing the propaganda war from within the residence, the rebels chanted together, unfurled a new banner and shouted slogans to reporters outside.

"We will carry on until we die. We will not back down in our efforts," they shouted, local Radio Programas del Peru said. "The families of our prisoners are also waiting for them in their homes. Peace for all Peruvians," read the banner's message, in blue letters on a white bed sheet.
With no visible activity on negotiations, police have intensified their war of nerves with the MRTA.

Apart from the helicopter, armoured personnel carriers with heavy machine guns have in recent days passed within a few blocks of the residence, while police have approached the walls, tossed stones into the driveway, peeked around the gate and run backward and forward in a seeming effort to unnerve the MRTA.

The MRTA rebels, whose movement is named for an 18th century Indian leader who led an uprising against Spanish colonial rule, originally seized hundreds of guests when they stormed a cocktail party at the residence on Dec. 17.

They freed most in what they called "goodwill gestures," keeping those they consider the most important bargaining chips, including two Peruvian Cabinet ministers, generals, security chiefs, about two dozen Japanese businessmen and diplomats and ambassadors from Bolivia and Japan.

Fujimori, whose brother Pedro is also among the captives, told the Japanese reporters he could consider secondary MRTA demands for improved jail conditions for their comrades and political asylum for themselves in another country. "It is a question of listening and giving suggestions," he said.
He travelled Thursday to La Paz for a meeting with his Bolivian counterpart, Gonzalo Sanchez de Lozada.

The MRTA is holding Bolivia's ambassador to Peru in the hope of obtaining the release of four rebels jailed in the neighbouring country. But Bolivia has from the outset backed Fujimori's stance on prisoners.
